Cultivate

/KUL-tih-vayt/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Cultivate means to nurture, develop, or improve through sustained effort.

Cultivate means to nurture, develop, or improve through sustained effort. Over four seasons the young pitcher cultivated a changeup that no batter in the league could read.

Worked Example

When Ivy moved to the city, she knew exactly two people. Instead of waiting for friendships to happen, she worked at them. She hosted a monthly soup night even when only one guest came, remembered birthdays, and followed up on every 'we should get coffee sometime.' She joined the neighborhood cleanup crew and kept showing up through the cold months. Five years later, her kitchen table needed both leaves for soup night — a circle of friends she had deliberately cultivated.

Ivy's friendships grow because she tends them with sustained, deliberate effort over years — hosting, remembering, following up — which is what it means to cultivate something.

Antonyms

How Strong Is It? — tend → cultivate → perfect

tend vs. cultivate

tend vs. cultivate: Tend is gentler and weaker — tending keeps something alive as it is; cultivating pushes it to grow and improve through sustained effort.

perfect vs. cultivate

perfect vs. cultivate: Perfect is stronger than cultivate: to perfect a skill is to finish its development completely, while cultivating is the long middle stretch of growth.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — cult

Root — cult: to till, to care for (Latin colere/cultus)

Suffix — -iv-

Suffix — -iv-: the connecting element from Medieval Latin cultivus, 'tilled' — it links the root to the verb ending

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: verb-forming: to make or do

Put it together

Put it together: Cult- (to till, to care for — Latin colere/cultus) + -iv- (the link from Medieval Latin cultivus, 'tilled') + -ate (verb-forming) = to work at tending something. Farmers cultivated fields; later, English speakers cultivated minds, manners, and friendships by the same logic of patient tending. The root thrives in agriculture (field-tilling) and culture — originally 'that which is carefully grown.'

Use the root in a new word: culture

Use the root in a new word: culture: A lab technician grows a bacterial culture in a warm dish — culture, from Latin colere (to till, to care for), is literally something carefully grown, just as a cultivated talent is.
